newsitem.title: UK: Activists want to show dead foetuses on British TV.
newsitem.headline: Activists want to show dead foetuses on British TV.

text.p: Anti-abortion activists said on Wednesday they had gathered enough candidates to win national air time in Britain's election campaign and hoped to use their five-minute slot to show U.S. footage of dead foetuses.

The election takes place on May 1 but no firm date has yet been set for pre-polling broadcasts. Media experts could recall few precedents of such a graphic video being shown in Britain, which has no precedent for abortion politics.
"There are some women who will suffer trauma as a result of watching the broadcast," said Dr Michael Jarmulowicz, who is backing the anti-abortion campaign.
But the Pro-Life Alliance, a one-issue group that has never fielded candidates before, said it would stop short of showing film of an actual abortion. Britain, it said, was not ready.
"Our aim is not to use shock tactics, just to reveal the truth of the situation," said the group's Jonathan Stephens. "We want to campaign on the reality of what happens in an abortion."
Stephens said the dead foetuses ranged from 24 weeks old to full-term babies, which are born at about 40 weeks.
He said fellow activists in the United States, where abortion politics are far more ingrained in the electoral sytem, found the foetuses in waste sacks outside a clinic in Texas.
"Pro-lifers found these foetuses in garbage dumpsters out back just like any other waste," he said. "It's shocking when you see what happens to humanity."

Any party fielding 50 candidates is entitled to one five-minute slot on national television but it was not clear how much, if any, of the footage could be aired on British television, which operates under strict guidelines.

"Until it is broadcast we can't know what the audience reaction will be or what decision we would ultimately take. We do occasionally get complaints about news footage involving death, destruction and large-scale tragedy but the question tends to be more about the timing than the content," said Clare Reynolds of the Broadcasting Standards Council.
It would be up to the Independent Television Network and BBC to decide what footage could actually be shown.
But whatever is finally aired, the group has achieved its aim to join the established parties and win national air time.

"At this point we have 53 candidates with confirmed constituencies. We have a further three, whose constituencies are to be announced, plus we are in negotiation with other people about more seats," Stephens said. "We have achieved national broadcast time, which surprised many."
Unlike in the United States and many Catholic countries in Europe, abortion has been a political sideline in Britain, where members of parliament can largely vote with their conscience.
And while the foetus video originated in the United States, the privately-funded alliance has sought to distance itself from the confrontation and violence that have shaped the U.S. debate.
